item.title: Security Reference
item.description:
This page states how keys, keychains, tokens, and sessions behave, exactly, as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280. For the model, read the Keys, Keychains, Sessions, and Tokens concepts. For tasks, use the security guides. For base URL, authentication, and the organization header, see the Cloud API. All paths below sit under /api unless noted.

Permission keys 🔗

Provider Admin holds every key. The table lists the default holders of the other roles. “Interface” means the control or tab is disabled or replaced by a permission error screen. “Server” means the Layer5 Cloud server refuses the request with HTTP 403.

item.title: Build a Custom Keychain
item.description:
A custom keychain bundles the keys that a custom role needs. This guide creates a keychain, changes its keys, and deletes it. It is written for Provider Admins and self-hosted operators, because only a Provider Admin can create, change, or delete a keychain, or include it in a role. For the model, read the Keychains concept.

Before you start 🔗

  • You need the Provider Admin role. The interface also checks the Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, and Delete Keychain permissions for the matching controls. Provider Admin holds all three. No other default role does.
  • A keychain does nothing until a role includes it. Creating and editing roles is a Provider Admin action. On hosted Layer5 Cloud an organization cannot complete this path alone. On a self-hosted deployment, your Provider Admins can.
  • Keychains are not organization-scoped. A role that includes your keychain grants its keys to every user who holds that role, in every organization.

Create a keychain 🔗

Open the Keychains tab under Security and create a keychain. Give it a name and choose the keys it bundles. Layer5 Cloud creates the keychain and adds each key to it. If adding a key fails, the interface reports it as “Failed to add key to keychain”. Open the keychain and confirm every key you chose is present.

item.title: Keys
item.description:
A key is a named permission for exactly one action, such as Create Organization, Approve Catalog Request, or Download Token. Every authorization decision in Layer5 Cloud comes down to one question: does this user hold the key this action requires, in this organization? Understanding keys tells you why a user can or cannot do something, and whether the model fits the access rules you need.

How a key reaches a user 🔗

Keys roll up in three layers. A keychain groups related keys, a role groups keychains, and a user holds roles in an organization or a team. A user never receives a key directly: granting a key means placing it in a keychain that belongs to a role the user holds.
